newsitem.title: USA: Troop plan for Zaire may be changed - Perry.
newsitem.headline: Troop plan for Zaire may be changed - Perry.

text.p: Defense Secretary William Perry said on Saturday that the United States and its allies might modify a plan to send troops to Zaire next week because of the return of thousands of refugees to Rwanda from Zaire.
"There have been some very interesting and positive developments in Zaire in the last two days," Perry told a news conference. "It is possible that our plan, the allied plan ... will be modified."

He said a U.S. assessment team in the region would report to Washington quickly on the need for troops, promised by the United States and some 20 other nations under U.N. auspices to support humanitarian aid to a million refugees in Zaire.

But tens of thousands of the those refugees, who faced danger from starvation and disaese, have in the past two days begun streaming from camps near Goma and other areas of eastern Zaire back into Rwanda.
"If this trend continues, it will change substantially the nature of the humanitarian problem" in Zaire, said Perry.
"It will not eliminate the need for humanitarian support, but it will substantially change the nature of that need," he said.
Perry stressed that no changes had been made yet in the tentative U.S. offer to send 1,000 troops to Goma and several thousand other support personnel to countries neighboring Zaire.

He said Washington would consult with its allies after receiving reports from the 40-member U.S. military survey team in the area this weekend. That team also includes representatives from Britain, France and Canada.
"We are standing by in a ready mode to move forward with humanitarian support," said Perry.
"Just as soon as we get detailed information from our survey team about what the precise situation on the ground is, we will make our decision and move."

President Bill Clinton said this week that he had agreed tentatively to send 1,000 troops to Goma to secure the airport and set up a corridor two miles (3 km) long from Goma into Rwanda so that food and other aid as well as refugees could move freely.
That U.S. commitment was conditioned on getting assurances that the scope and duration of the humanitarian relief mission would be specific and limited, among other demands.

Reports of a sudden mass movement of Rwandan refugees toward home raised questions of whether this might eliminate the need for an international relief mission, but Clinton said on Friday it would be premature to draw any such conclusion.

He promised that U.S. troops would be authorized to defend themselves with firepower if the United States joined the proposed Canadian-led international force to provide security for civilian relief agencies trying to help the refugees.

He said such rules of engagement were essential to any humanitarian military mission, and referred to what he called the successful international mission to the former Yugoslavia as evidence that such rules work.
